title: Proteomic insights into human induced regulatory T cells: the role of LPXN and CD160 in immune suppression
projectDescription: Regulatory T cells (Tregs) play a central role in maintaining immune homeostasis, and the implementation of in vitro induced Treg cells (iTreg) to control immune function has significant potential in clinical medicine. The clinical application of iTregs has been limited by their poor stability. To better define the molecular characteristics of human iTregs, we performed a data-independent acquisition proteomics, detecting over 8000 proteins and providing a quantitative comparison of their relative levels in iTregs and activated Th0 cells. Consistent with the known molecular characteristics of Tregs, several Treg signature proteins, including FOXP3, Eos, IL2RA, CTLA4, PD-1, Aiolos, LAG3, RUNX1 and HIC1, were identified and validated using targeted proteomics and/or qRT-PCR. Notably, leupaxin (LPXN) level was upregulated during Treg cell differentiation. Functional studies demonstrated that LPXN-deficient cells showed impaired expression of Treg protein markers FOXP3, Eos and IKZF3 and impaired suppression of effector T cells. In addition, we identified a distinct CD160⁺ iTregs subpopulation characterized by a distinct proteomic signature as compared to CD160⁻ iTregs. Together, these findings provide a high-resolution proteomic landscape of human iTregs and identified a novel role of LPXN in the development and suppressive activity of iTregs.
sampleProcessingProtocol: The iTregs and control Th0 cells were collected in LoBind tubes (Eppendorf), washed with PBS, and lysed in a buffer containing 100 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0) and 4% SDS. Following sonication and centrifugation at 16,000 × g, the protein-containing supernatant was collected and stored at −80°C. For proteomic analysis, lysates were reduced with dithiothreitol (DTT) and alkylated with iodoacetamide (IAA). Protein digestion was performed using the suspension-trapping (S-Trap™) method. Briefly, DTT and IAA treated lysates were acidified with phosphoric acid, mixed with binding buffer (90% methanol, 100 mM triethylammonium bicarbonate; TEAB, pH 7.1), and loaded onto S-Trap™ columns. After centrifugation, columns were washed with binding buffer, and proteins were digested overnight at 37°C with MS-grade trypsin. Peptides were recovered by stepwise elution and resuspended in 2% acetonitrile / 0.1% formic acid for subsequent LC–MS/MS analysis.
dataProcessingProtocol:
The resuspended peptides (800 ng) were analyzed using an EasynLC 1200 system coupled to an Orbitrap Exploris™ 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Peptides were loaded onto a pre-column (20 x 0.1 mm) and separated over a 120-minute gradient on a 75 µm x 25 cm analytical column (packed in-house with 3 µm Reprosil C18; Dr Maisch GmbH). Gradient elution was performed at a flow rate of 300 nL/min, with the solvent B composition ranging from 5% to 21% in 62 min, up to 36% in 48 min, and to 100 % in 5 min, with a final 5-minute isocratic composition. The mobile phase consisted of water with 0.1% formic acid (A) and 80% acetonitrile with 0.1% formic acid (B). The column was maintained at 60°C using an in-house built oven (30). 
The LC-MS configuration combined a high-field asymmetric ion mobility spectrometry (FAIMS) interface, which was operated with two compensation voltages, –40 V and –60 V. Data Independent Analysis was performed in positive mode with a mass resolution of 120k, scan range of 395-1005 m/z, AGC target of 700000, and cycle time of 3 sec, with a maximum injection time of 50 ms. The MS/MS scan range was set to 180-2000 m/z, with loop control set to All. Normalized collision energy was set to 30%, Orbitrap resolution to 30k, maximum injection time of 52 ms, and AGC target to custom.
Raw files were converted to htrms files using the htrms converter (Biognosys), followed by directDIA database search using Spectronaut (v18, Biognosys). Trypsin/P was selected as the digestion enzyme, with carbamidomethylation selected as a fixed modification, and methionine oxidation and N-terminal acetylation selected as variable modifications. False discovery rates (FDRs) were set to 0.01.

To further characterize the CD160+ and CD160– sorted iTregs, DIA-MS analysis was performed using the EasynLC 1200 and Orbitrap Exploris™ 480 mass spectrometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific), as described above.
